subtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext: The discussion had better take place now, otherwise there can-
not 'be a general discussion on the principle of the Bill.
I shall he quite satisfied.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Under the rules of the House, hon. members should have taken advantage of the second reading to discuss the principle of the Bill. It is only with the unanimous consent of the Committee that this general discussion ipay take place now. When it has been completed, I hope the Chairman will have the assistance of hon. members in securing the observance of section 5 of rule 13.
Mr.- MOWAT: I would like to say how gratifying it is to many members of the House that the Government has seen fit to bring in a Bill of this nature. The measure is bound to be unpopular in certain quarters because of its radical provisions, but for that reason the Government is entitled to all the greater credit for having brought it forward. Did we not have a Union Government in Canada at the present time I doubt very much whether we should have seen such a Bill introduced, in view of the manner in which the Civil Service has been administered for so many years. The fact that it has done so is to me a proof that it does not fear unpopularity. For that reason I am glad to be a supporter, for the time being, of a Union Government. Legislation of this kind is bound to make the Government unpopular in certain directions. I am glad, for one, even if unpopularity should result, because it will demonstrate to the people that even at the risk of unpopularity the Government will enact such measures at it believes to be in the interest of the country as a whole.
We are only beginning here a policy which was inaugurated in older countries many years ago and hon. gentlemen will perhaps pardon me if I give a short resume of what has transpired in Great Britain with respect to this important question. As far back as 1823, nearly a hundred years ago, the evils of patronage were first drawn attention to in the British House of Commons. At that time Lord John Russell made use of these remarks:
Offices in the Post Office and Customs are made part of the patronage of members voting with the Government. When an office is vacant the Minister seeing his advantage, writes to the member for the county and asks his recommendation.
In 1829, the Duke of Wellington said:
The whole system of the patronage is, in my opinion, erroneous.
	*
Coming down to 1849, we find that competent old statesman, Sir Charles Trevelyan, taking special charge of the question of Civil Service and of patronage. He said in a repont of that year:
The dregs of ail other professions, and young men who have no chance in open competition are attracted towards the Civil Service, as to a secure asylum.
Readers of Charles Dickens, who are familiar with the novel " Little Dorrit," will recall how he described the efforts made by Arthur Clennam to interest himself, and how Little Dorrit was uneasy, -and her great fear was that he was entering upon ia dangerous proceeding. That exhibits the Civil Service as it was then. You will remember how Clennam went to the Circumlocution Office and first saw the son of -Mr. Tite Barnacle, and how young Barnacle treated him when he began the *sentence, " I want to know "- Young Barnacle said: "My dear fellow, you must not come round here saying ' I want to know,' you know, because that's very irregular." And' so on, and how Clennam was passed down to Wobbler and then to Tite Barnacle at his house, and on to Clive, then how the old man in the other office advised him very tenderly not to proceed with the inquiry he was making because it would take a lifetime to get an answer. The writings of Charles Dickens exercised great influence in the change in the Civil Service in England. Then, in 1855, there was a joint report by Sir Stafford Northcote and Sir Charles Trevelyan, which provided for a personal examination to qualify only, and this is the same law as we have at the present time with regard to what is called the Outside Service. In the second place, it precluded a commission for interfering with the appointment of those who had the duty of nomination or appointment, and finally provided for the appointment of mature persons without examination. This consequently did not take the whole of the patronage away from political control.
Then Mr. Layard, afterwards Sir Henry Layard, moved a resolution with respect to merit and efficiency having been sacrificed in public appointments to party and family influences and to a blind adherence to routine which threatened to bring discredit upon the national character.
In 1860 a select committee recommended that a moderate and modified competition be held for these appointments. In 1870, which is a record year in the history of the Civil Service, Mr. Lowe, who

afterwards became Lord Sherbrooke, approved an Order in Council making competitive tests obligatory in certain departments of the Civil Service, and he sard- and with this I think many in this House will agree at the present time:
Men who up to twenty-two years have been in no business or profession are superior to men who at eighteen have devoted themselves to the special duties of their calling.
In other words he believed that the best kind of civil servant was a man trained not only in business but in general literature and education, and who was not appointed until a more mature age. Such a man is more valuable to the state than one who entered the service and learned the routine of business at a very young age. In 1874, under Mr. Gladstone, as a result of the work of the Playfair Commission, the Civil Service was divided into four classes. First, administrative officers, appointed by promotion on account of their ability. Sec-eond, those in the higher branches of the Civil Service who obtained their offices by competitive examination. The third class were those for the lower branches appointed after a simpler competitive examination. The fourth class were the men on day wages who were appointed upon a qualifying examination only. In 1876, followed an Order in Council providing for a higher scale of pay. Then, in 1890, Sir Matthew White Ridley's Commission mentioned that men of more liberal culture were required, and that certain special appointments required men of professional and technical knowledge. In 1910, an Order in Council was passed, amending and consolidating former Orders, and which may be looked upon as the code of Civil Service regulation in the British Empire. "
Mr. A. IC. MACLEAN: That was in 1910?

Yes. In 1914, a very important report was made by leading members of all classes, including our present Governor General, the Duke of Devonshire, who devoted a good deal of thought and consideration to the report, and who, at times, dissented in minority reports from the majority of the committee. Some other members were Lord Macdonell, a very competent and distinguished civil servant; Mr. Philip Snowdon, representing the Labour party or the socialist branch of it; and Mrs. Streatfield, representing the women of the country, who have more and more shown their ability to become efficient public servants. Their report is most comprehensive in dealing with the whole question both in 109i
theory and in practice, and reference to it may be of great value to those who are considering this question. '
I prdpose to quote some extracts to the House for the purpose of emphasizing the importance of making the Civil Service of Canada not a mere trade or employment, but a profession. There is no reason why men should not go into the Civil Service profession as they go into medicine, law or engineering, because the Civil Service of Canada includes men who must be scientific in many branches, in matters of marine, of fisheries, of militia, of justice, copyright patents, and so. We cannot ex-
5 p.m. pect to obtain the best type of men unless we dignify the iser-vice and put it on a higher plane, taking it away from the influence of party politics, and giving opportunity for promotion and for increase in emolument, so that a civil servant can bring up his family in decency and give his children a good education. He cannot expect to do that unless we have a Bill which contains the principle of the Bill now 1 before the House. It is a dreadful thing to me to think of a man, perhaps a graduate of a university, spending many years perfecting himself in the details of his department, studying the general literature which pertains to that department, giving his whole life to the service of his country in the Civil Service, having some one appointed over him because that person has had more practical experience in the political field and must receive a party	reward. While	men of
that kind may be quite	as good
public servants as others-and it has proven so in our present public service- yet, taking the general run of things, the man who has devoted himself to the affairs of practical politics, and has acquired an influence which has enabled him to he shoved into the Civil Service, is not likely to be as valuable to the country as the man who has given his life to the profession. Therefore, it is gratifying to many members of the House on both sides, I am sure, that the Government have seen fit at last, after years of experiment in the Old Country and the United 'Stateis, to bring in a measure of this range and character.
Mr. Dorman B. Eaton, who was Chairman, I think, of a House of Representatives Civil Service Commission in the United States in 1880, made these remarks upon the state of affairs which had come into existence with regard to their Civil Service. After the war an innumerable number of men besieged the departments at

Washington to exercise their influence to secure appointments both for themselves and their friends, and the Civil Service got into a sorry plight; and American statesmen saw that they could not go on like that, that the public offices were overmanned, filled with incompetents and with men who did not give their whole time to the performance of their duties, and who could evade their strict duty because of the political influence they could bring to bear upon the heads of the departments. Mr. Dorman B. Baton said this:
Patronage creates a mercenary political class, an oligarchy of stipendiaries, a bureaucracy of the worst kind, which controls parties with relentless despotism, imposing upon them at the election issues which are prescribed not by the actual feeling and interest of the country, but solely by the necessities and profit of the oligarcy, while to secure this advantage, party spirit, the constant and mortal enemy of
republics, is inflamed to the utmost	
This system disgusts with politics and repels from them good citizens who cannot compete with the professional political class which gives all its time to a pursuit by which it profits.
While I do not say by any means that our Civil Service has got into any such direful condition as is depicted in that description, yet that is that tendency provided we go on with our present system. I* is quite true that many of the best citizens of our country have not 'a high opinion of our political institutions and have a distrust of the doings of politicians, in the House of Commons or the Senate, or in the Civil Service.
The reason probably is that he is unable to exercise any influence upon it; his relatives or his sons should, in his opinion, because of their possessing abilities superior to those of many public servants, have a chance to enter the Civil Service, but because they are not party politicians they cannot get a place.
The Civil Service would benefit by a system of competitive examination in the Outside Service. Since 1908 a system, of competitive examination has been followed in the Inside Service, but in the Outside Service the examination has been merely a qualifying one and is quite insufficient. The Outside Service should have the same standing as the Inside Service. The practical result of a system of competitive examination in the Outside as well as the Inside Service would be the establishing of a public service consisting of a better class of employees than those who have hitherto been appointed. It array be said that a man who, because of his peculiar facility for answering examination questions and hie kno-wledge of school and college work, may

get a good place in a Civil Service examination, and yet may not be sufficiently practical or have the qualifications required of an efficient employee in the public service. That may be true in a few cases, but what we are trying to get at is a general principle under which we may arrive at the best results. The Civil Service Commission in England, which is composed of some of the best statesmen of that country, was correct when it reported that, on the whole, men who as a result of their school and college work succeeded in the Civil Service examinations made the most competent civil servants. So that if we get nothing else from this' Bill than a system of examination for the Outside Service, we shall bring about good results. Some men who have J>een politicians and who are no-w in the Service have done well; we all know who and how competent they are; I need not mention names. But men in the Service with ambition to go ahead; men who desire to increase their efficiency and their standing, are dulled and frozen in the attempt; they become mere drones, doing their work day by day without hope of promotion or of increase in their salaries or standing; without hope of satisfying their reasonable ambition to become successful men as have their compeers and companions- in the ranks . of the private professions.
The working out of this Bill will produce complications at first; will give rise to troubles and irritations because of its newness. The same thing happened in England; the men of one department were known to resign in a body because they considered themselves unfairly treated. The member of Parliament became disgusted' because his influence waned and he felt receding from him the committees which had steadfastly supported him in his constituency because they knew that Civil Service appointments would be given them or their relatives and friends. But the member acquired) a new political backing; he acquired committees of a new kind and has been able to get very efficient political services from them-but not from those who expect to be Civil Servants. While the change, therefore, may cause temporary inconvenience and give rise to temporary irritations and opposition on the part of politicians, in a very few years it will so work out that the Service will be bene-fitted and political patronage will be forever eliminated.
A good feature of the Bill is that the status of those who are at present Civil Servants shall not be interfered with. This takes away a good deal of opposition to the

Bill. The Civil Servants of Ottawa, of whom there are now thousands, welcome this Bill with enthusiasm-not the mere class enthusiasm which might be called selfish, but the enthusiasm of men who have thought on these subjects for years, and who have groaned under the inequalities and injustices of the Service. Undoubtedly these injustices have not been deliberate; they have arisen of necessity through various circumstances connected with our present system.
Under this Bill all appointments are relegated to a commission. We do not expect the commission at once to produce the condition of affairs in the public service which prevails in older countries, but we anticipate that by fair attention to their duties, by an intelligent grasp of the needs of the Service and by loyal *support of 'the principles embodied in this Bill, they will eventually enable us to be freed from the injustices and inefficiency which have prevailed in many branches of the Service since 'Confederation.
Unquestionably a Civil Service Commission sitting in Ottawa cannot be expected to know the personal characteristics of their appointees; in that respect they will have to depend upon reports of post office inspectors, collectors of customs and other leading officials in the Service throughout the country.
I hope that the circumstances will not resnlt in the impression being created that once .a man passes an examination he is given a life job. Nothing could he more hurtful to the interests of the Service. If there is one 'thing that is a nuisance in this country it is the curt, impolite, grudging public servant. He does' exist in places; we all know him and we have all been troubled by him. If a public servant of this kind is the result of the system of political appointments, then we can none too soon get rid of the system. The public servant should understand that it is his duty to be courteous and obliging, and if this Bill fails to reach that phase of the subject the principle of efficiency in the public service cannot be fully carried out. We must have men not only who understand the duties of their office, but who have common sense, who will take the trouble to satisfy the public with whom they deal. This result is much more apt to be obtained under a commission, which, on complaint being made regarding the manners or inattention of a public servant, have power at once to " sit upon him '* and thus to make it generally known that the administration
of the Civil Service is in charge of a businesslike commission which will see to it that public servants attend to their duties as they should.
On the whole, I congratulate the Government and, in particular, the Acting Minister of Finance who introduced this Bill, on their courage in attacking a grievance, belated as this action may be. We are, of course, not yet a great country, and we naturally must be somewhat imitative of others. We all regret that. .1 regret that we have not, to any great extent, customs and fashions of our own. We depend largely upon what goes on in other countries. The great country to the south of us is richer than we are, and it has a very active life; it has its own fashions and customs, and we are naturally inclined to copy them rather than t-o have our own. I sometimes wish we copied the customs of some oldeT countries rather than those of newer countries, because we often imitate what is bad in the newer country to the South of us instead of what is good in it. Be that as it may, we cannot help being imitative, and we have now reached a stage when we are getting into this frame of mind, that we must have a modern Civil Service Bill of our own. We are ceasing to take things haphazard. By this concrete code of regulations, because that is what the Civil Service Bill amounts to; I believe we shall do good to our country and to the Civil Service; we shall elevate the Civil Service to a position it has never had before; we shall give new heart to those who have laboured for years in the service, and ten years from now, when this legislation works out as I hope it will, under the Civil Service Commission, we shall wonder why we ever permitted so long things to go on in their present shape.

I desire heartily to concur in the remarks that have been made with regard to the wisdom of the measure brought down by the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. A. K. Maclean), and at the same time to agree very largely with what my hon. friend from Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) has just said. I am pleased that the minister has allowed a little general discussion. I desire, in the first place, to approve entirely the principle of the Bill, and I think it would have been well if, in Canada, we could have had this legislation at an earlier date than this. The salaries paid in nearly all of the departments of the Government are less than they should be. Particularly is that the case in the Outside 'Service with which I am more

familiar than. I am with the salaries paid to civil servants in the city of Ottawa. But I believe, to a less or greater extent, it prevails in all branches of the service that, during war time, the men who have had to live on fixed salaries, have had very much the worst of it. 'The very high cost of living has not enabled those men to live in the comfort in which they lived in prewar days. The advances that have been made in the various branches of the Civil Service are not such as; in my judgment, should have been made, nor have they been made as readily as they should. I speak with a good deal of feeling in regard to this phase of the question. What I say is particularly true of the Post Office Department. I think within the last two years at least ten representations have been sent in to the Post Office Department as to the under-payment of letter carriers and clerks in our cities and towns. The salaries of those men are not at all commensurate with the very important work they have to do. They are entrusted with handling registered letters, money orders, postal notes and thousands of dollars' worth of other valuable property in the way of parcels, and yet their scale of pay is not as high as an ordinary labouring man could get at the present time. Further, during this war time, men, have been employed in the post office in my own district, the city of Brantford, for three land a half years, and the are still called temporaries. When the law was made in regard to temporary employees, a man was not allowed to be employed temporarily in the post office for more than six months at any one time or in any one year. That was, in my opinion a very strange law in itself; yet there are men who, during the war, have beeen acting as temporary clerks or letter carriers, that are still on the non-permanent staff and that are paid on the basis of temporary employees, and, in some cases, uniforms are not supplied as they are to the permanent letter carriers. That sort of thing should have ceased long ago, and I have put in very strong representations to all the Acting Pastmaster Generals that we have had in such plenty during the last two or three years. I regret we have not a Postmaster General to whom we can go and talk, and whom we can get to rectify these matters, but we have been in that position for a long time. I have, within the last six months, had five or si$ deputations on this matter alone, and I have told those deputations I shall do all I possibly can. I, therefore, take this first opportunity of impressing upon the [iMr. Cockahutt.]
Acting Minister of Finance, who, for the moment, controls the purse-strings of the public treasury, that he limber up a little on them, and that all of our permanent staff, whether they be in the city of Ottawa or in any of the outlying cities of Canada, or in the country districts, down to the man who carries the rural mail and the man who receives $30 a year for furnishing a place for a post office and for lighting and heating it, should receive better consideration. The whole Service is run on far too parsimonious a scale for the public to get the service we should receive. I am strongly in favour of having an all round advance for efficient service, and wherever service is not efficient, I would get rid of it. That is the way I do in business. I believe with my hon. friend (Mr. Mowat) that a man in a public office should be just as civil as if he had half a dozen others to compete with. Some public servants, by their attitude, seem to say: You can come or go; you can take this, or that, and that is all you are going to get; you will have to do as I choose, or you will not do business with me. That should not be. A civil servant is given a position to serve the public courteously, and courtesy should be insisted on in every branch of the Civil Service. Most of our civil servants treat the public in a courteous manner, but there are some who do not. I should like to see this question of pay and this question of courteous treatment to the public receive attention, and I believe that the system of promotion for fitness, for efficiency, should, as far as possible, be carried out. A man who has been doing good service should be given promotion. I have endeavoured to make myself clear in regard to the matter of recompense. I have not read the Bill very carefully all through, but I do not think the salaries to be paid are specified.
As a member of Parliament I am glad to be relieved of the responsibility of the Civil Service as embraced in my own riding. But there are some few points which, as a practical politician, I wish to fully understand. I am trying to be practical. In the first place the members of the Civil Service	Commission are located in Ottawa. I have the pleasure of knowing several of them, *and I believe they are very capable men. The Civil Service of Canada is paid by the people of all Canada, and not by the people of Ottawa, and I think every electoral district throughout the Dominion is entitled to a fair quota of men from that particular district. I Lay that down as a principle. I

think the members of this House and the people of this country will have every reason to be dissatisfied if the appointment of the Civil Service Commission is going to mean that the members* of the Civil Service in all the towns and cities from east to west and north to south lare going to be sent from the city of Ottawa. I do not know whether that is the intention or not, but I want the minister to guard against that. I lay down as* a principle that every riding is entitled to a certain number of its own people to administer its own business, subject to the rules and regulations laid down by the Civil Service Commission. That may be considered rather a narrow view, but I think .it is a practical opinion. I think in all our communities we have men who are fit to discharge the various duties in all walks of life ,and I think the people of Ottawa, as fair-minded people, should not want to add to the eight or ten or fifteen thousand people they now have in Ottawa, and they are mostly Ottawa people, the appointments in every city and town and in every country district throughout the Dominion. I think every electoral district is entitled to have a certain representation in the public service of Canada, and I hope I have the backing of my fellow-members in making what I believe to be a very fair contention with regard to the Outside Service, as it is called.
I understand from a question that was asked in the House the other diay by the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) and answered by the Prime Minister, that members may or may not be consulted. Though I was in the House at the time, I must say that the answer did not appear to me to carry very strong conviction either one way or the other as to whether the member for a constituency was a proper man to be consulted as to who w.as fit to serve in any given position. If a m.ember is not a fit man to* be consulted in that matter, I think it is a reflection on his judgment and* on his standing in his own community. If he is not .a fit person I do not know who the fit man in that constituency would be to be consulted. I personally do not want to be charged with the making of appointments. It has got me into more trouble than it has ever done me good, because for every position to fill there are ten or twenty applications, hut I say that if the members of this commission want the best testimony that can be got in the average constituency, they cannot go to a better man than the member
elected for that constituency. I do not want to be considered as blowing my own trumpet; not at all. But the very fact that a member has the confidence of the majority of his constituents is a reason why he is entitled to he consulted. I do not say that his selection should he final by any means.
I think the great trouble in the past has been that members in order to pay some political debt, or for some other reason of a more or less sordid character, have not used their best judgment in making nominations, owing to pressure perhaps or some other reason. But if the member will use his best judgment he can make a recommendation that will reflect credit on the position to be filled and credit on his judgment in the selection. But if this commission are not going to consult the member for a constituency, he should certainly be relieved from all responsibility for the administration of those offices. As it is now, if there is anything wrong in the post office, customs, inland revenue, or any other department, who hears about it first? The man who has a complaint to make runs direct to the member and says: "You are supporting the Government that is giving us this administration." The trouble comes home to roost with the member at once. The principle should be this: If members are not consulted, or, being consulted, their advice is not followed, the Civil Service Commission or the Government, who stand back of them, should relieve the member of the responsibility for seeing any particular office administered as it should be. I believe first, that members *axe fit * and proper persons to be consulted, and that having been consulted, their advice should be .followed, unless for some good reason. If a member is not consulted, he should he relieved from responsibility for any action taken by the commission or whoever may make the appointment.
A man who gets a position in the public service is required to pass an examination. It may be a fairly stiff one, and that is where the outlying districts are at a disadvantage again. Here in Ottawa a large numbeT of young imen and women will be passing examinations all the time, but in the country districts the people do not hear about the vacancy until the time in which to apply has expired. There is another point. A young man or a young woman may qualify for a position in the public service by passing an examination with high honours, and then find themselves without a job. How long are they to be kept waiting? That is a .question

for consideration!. There should be a reasonable time beyond which the young men or young women who have qualified themselves for the public service should not be kept waiting. At present they may be kept waiting months or years, and eventually get tired of waiting and take something else. I do not find in the Bill any guarantee that if a young man or woman qualifies he will necessarily get a job. It appears to me there should be in every community a certain number qualifying for the positions likely to become vacant in that district, and when they have qualified themselves their cases should receive first consideration when the vacancy occurs. No outsider should be sent in until all avenues have been tried for finding a man in the riding; that is the proposition I lay down, and I think it is a perfectly proper one.
The personnel of the commission is, I think, a good one. I have the honour of knowing the chairman. He was for many years a member of this House and a minister of the Crown. He is a fair-minded, reasonable man, and I think he will endeavour to give a good account of himself.
I also know another member of the commission, and I think we are safe in their hands, so far as we can be safe under certain rules. But it must be remembered they are going to be guided by these rules, and while we all wish to have proper rules set up, they should be elastic enough to enable the commissioners to take a broad view of the matter, to recognize that it is not the money of the people of Ottawa that is being expended but the money of the people of all Canada. We are all interested in having our public servants fairly paid, and in trying to avoid a feeling of discontent and disquiet because their reasonable wants have not been met, and I do not think they have been met in the past.
I think we would do well if we got the Civil Service on a basis similar to the Civil Service in England; that we should advance our public servants gradually step by step as their length of service and ability warrants, and then they would have something to look forward to. At the present time there are men who have been thirty and forty years in the service at the same old job, and have had practically no advance to speak of during that thirty or forty years, and now in their declining years they have very little to retire on. Some get a small pension and others .nothing at all. The whole question should be taken up m a very comprehensive way.' Full salaries

should be paid for the present and the retiring allowance should be arranged for the man, or the woman, in this particular walk of life. We will have a much larger number of women in the public service in the immediate future than we have had in the past. A retiring allowance or a pension should be provided so that those people who have served the public long and faithfully may spend their declining years in comparative ease and comfort.

I confess that I am very pleased to see the Government introduce a Civil Service Bill that will take appointments out of party politics. I think they could not do anything better. I have not had an opportunity of reading the Bill through and I do not know what its provisions are in their entirety but I noticed one clause to which I should like to invite the attention of the committee. It provides that, where a civil servant is transferred from one department to the other, if, in the department to which he is transferred, the salary is lower, he must go in at the lower salary. I think that i,c absolutely unfair. There is another clause saying that he shall be entitled within a certain time to increases up to the salary that he received in the position which he formerly held but in the meantime, when transferred, he must accept the lower salary. I repeat, that is unfair. I do not think that clause should go through.
As to the 'Civil Service Commission, I do not know whether they are fairminded men or not, but if they are not fairminded men we are putting ,a lot of power in their hands because influence might be exerted underneath the surface1 that ordinary people would not know anything about. If they are subject to that sort of thing, we had better consider before putting so much power in their hands. However, I take it that the idea and intention of the Government is that these men shall be absolutely unbiased and fair. But, if there is some secret influence by some members of the Government, or by some people who may be known to the commissioners', the system will be nothing but a curse and a nuisance. If they exercise this power fairly I am absolutely in favour of the Bill.
I am in favour anyway of giving it a trial. The laws that we make here are not like the laws of the Medes and Persians, we can change them next year if the commission do not do what is right. The hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) says that we members are more or less responsible for the conditions as they exist at the present time, but if this Bill passes we will not be

responsible any more, and then we can tell those people who .are clamouring for positions that we are not responsible and that they can go down to Ottawa and get after the Civil Service Commission with a gun, ot club, or anything they like. That will be a relief to us, and as far as that is concerned I am not worrying about it. I am willing to give the thing a trial, but I would like to have some of these clauses amended.
I am entirely in accord with the general principle of taking the Civil Service out of politics. It looks to me from such consideration as I have been able to give the Bill that there is too much power placed in the hands of the deputy ministers. Suppose that a man, or a girl, in the department offends the deputy in some way or other, he or she cannot get an increase of salary or a promotion without a recommendation from the deputy. I recently had something of that kind brought to my attention and I thought the young man in that case had been treated unfairly. I think we should give that clause our very serious consideration. Some of the deputies may he large-mined men and would not take a narrow view as to those who are in their department. On the other hand, there may toe deputies who are not so liberal in their views', and we are putting a great deal of .power in their hands when we say that a civil servant of any department can only get an increase of salary, or promotion, on the recommendation of the deputy. I think we should; also, consider the provision that a civil servant, upon being transferred from one ^department to the other, may toe required to- accept a lower salary. As I have already said, I am in full accord with the general .principle of the Bill.

As this is a general discussion, I desire to draw the attention of the House, and particularly the .attention of the Government, to one, matter which has already partially toeen discussed during the session, and that is the .position of those members of the Civil Service who are serving with His Majesty's forces. Under a late Order in Council, a copy of which I have not toeen able to obtain this afternoon, the civil pay of these men has been cut off and they are entitled now merely to their military pay and allowances, I have here what purports to toe a copy of the Order in Council and, for the purpose of discussion and without at all guaranteeing its correctness, I propose to read it.
1.	After the thirtieth day of June, 1918, the above mentioned Orders in Council shall be void and of no effect and no person in the civil employment of the Government absent upon service with the forces of His Majesty, or of any of His Majesty's Allies, shall receive any portion of the pay or salary which after that date would otherwise accrue in respect of such civil employment.
2.	Any person in the civil employment of the Government absent upon service with the forces of His Majesty, or of any of His Majesty's Allies, shall be entitled upon the conclusion of the latter service, to be restored to his position in the civil employment of the Government if he remains Qualified to discharge the duties appertaining to that position.
Now this question arose in a different manner during the Session of 1916 and I *cannot do better, by way of explanation, than to quote the answelr of the then Minister of Militia and Defence, the present hon. member .for Victoria and Haliburton (Sir Sam Hughes) in answer to a question put to him:
Sir Sam Hughes: The rule in force is that members of the Civil Service who enlistel in the army prior to the 1st of November last draw their salaries as civil servants and also their pay and allowances as soldiers. Those who have joined the colours since the 1st of November, 1915, receive their military pay and an additional amount which brings it up to the amount of their Civil Service salaries, if their salaries in the service were larger than their military pay.
I tihink that succinctly covers the ground and shows what the position o-f these men was when they enlisted and went abroad. Earlier in the Session, when the matter came up, and it came up because of that difference being made, the right hon. the Prime Minister ('Sir Robert Borden), as reported at page 822, Hansard 1916, is quoted as follows:
An Order in Council was passed in the early weeks of the war providing that persons in the Civil Service of Canada who enlisted for overseas service would be paid their salaries during the time they were so serving their country at the front. At that time it was not anticipated that the war would last so long, and we had before us at that time the example of municipal corporations and railway and other corporations throughout Canada that were proposing to do exactly the same thing. The idea was impressed on the Government that the country could hardly afford to be less generous with regard to men who were prepared to make the supreme sacrifice than private corporations throughout the country.
Then he goes on to explain the reason why the Order in Council was changed *and why the date of that change was fixed at the first of November, 1915 and adds the following:
Every civil servant who has enlisted on or since that date has enlisted under terms and conditions which were perfectly well known to him at the time.

and later on :
When the war did last for such a very considerable period, in view of the increased additional strain put on the public service by reason of the duration of the war and of the greatly increased number of men we are sending, we came to the conclusion that some change should be made, and it was made along that line.
That is to say, the civil servant, instead of getting his full civil pay in addition to his military pay, was given sufficient from the civil list to make up, with his military pay, the amount of salary he had formerly been receiving.
In the same discussion, Hon. Mr. Roche, the then Minister of 'the Interior, and now the Chairman of the Civil Service Commission, spoke as follows:
I have explained the reason. Substitutes for civil servants who have gone to the front have to be paid out of the war appropriation, and we felt that there was too big a drain on it. That was one reason that led us to make the change. Hon. members who have spoken seem to think that the present system is the proper one, that is, only to pay these men the difference between their military and their civil pay, but they wish to go further and reduce the pay of those who enlisted prior to the first of November. I do not agree with that proposition, because it would be a breach of contract. All those men enlisted on certain conditions, and, as they did so enlist and went overseas, to reduce their pay would not be doing justice to them; but we are not doing any injustice to those who have enlisted since the first of November, because they know in advance what pay they are going to receive.
In the ensuing debate several of the members expressed their opinion on the subject. One hon. gentleman, the member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), who has just sat down, spoke as follows;
If these men joined under a certain understanding or promise, I do not see how the Government can honourably go back on that promise any more than an individual could.
I am sorry I cannot advocate the cancellation of the first arrangement, because the men joined on the understanding that it would be carried out.
In other words, the member for North Oxford could not, and would not, agree that the men who first enlisted, prior to the. first of November, 1915, should be cut down to the basis of those who enlisted after that date.
In the same debate the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) said:
I think the Government should give notice in the future of any change which they intend making. Any bargain you have made should be lived up to. If a man has gone under certain conditions, the Government cannot break the engagement.
[Mr. Cronyn. j
Now, Mr. Chairman, you will understand from the Order in Council which I have read, that not only those men who enlisted at the outbreak of the war, or prior to the first of November, 1915, hut those who* enlisted subsequent to that date, are to lose their civil pay and have to be content with their military pay and allowances. I think I need only state that proposition to the House to secure the disapprobation of the majority of the members to that course. I cannot conceive of any excuse for doing what a former minister of the Crown has stated would .amount to a breach of contract. It does involve, of course, a considerable money outlay, and it may also be argued that it is a discrimination in favour of those men against any who have enlisted1, or may enlist either under the Military Service Act, or otherwise, since the Order in Council of 'the 5th of April. I do not think either of those reasons should prevail, or, indeed', should have any effect whatever. I do -not want to enlarge on it at this time, but I do urge the Government very seriously to reconsider their action in this respect, and acting on the suggestion of .a minister in the former debate who asked for a concrete proposal, I am going to submit a recommendation, which I believe would be entirely workable. They tell me there are not very many of those original men still at the front, or abroad, that many of them have returned! I think the Government should say to those of them who do not come within the terms of the Military Service Act, those of them who are not liable to conscription:	" We will withdraw you
if you so desire, from the front, and return you to your post in the Civil Service. But if you remain, you must remain upon tue terms of this new regulation, and' rece've only your military pay." That might take some little time, it would depend upon the numbers involved and the military positions held, but I think it would be dealing to some extent fairly with these men, and with the country as well. Many of them are married men who would certainly come within the Act. Some are over the age, and others might, for some reason or other, be exempt from the provisions of the Act. All of these men, in my opinion, should be given the option of returning and resuming their places in the Civil Service.
This Order in Council also appears to affect, according to the information given to me, those members of the Civil Ser-

*vice who have jbined the various postal corps throughout Canada. A copy of the Order which I read was sent to such a man who was employed in the postal corps of Military District No. 1, and who, up to the date of that Order, had been receiving a certain amount of pay from the Civil Service. He is now cut off and his statement is that he loses about $50 a month. He is a married man and he and his family cannot possibly live on the military pay of $1.10 a day and whatever other field allowances there may be. That man certainly should be given the option to return to civil life. There may not be many cases of that kind, but there is one under my hand to which that applies.
There is one other point in connection with this matter. As I understand it, although I have no authority to quote on the subject, all those civil servants who enlisted did so upon the understanding that upon their return they should be reinstated (provided they were fit of course), in the situations they held, but at the salary which they would' have normally received had they remained in the country. The civil servants, I should judge from the Bill before us, get certain yearly increases up to a maximum amount, and a man who went away receiving a salary of $1,000 and remained away three years would' come back expecting to find his salary increased to $1,150 or $1,300. If his annual increase was $50 it would be the smaller sum, and if the yearly increase was $100 it would be the. larger amount. Now, I am informed that in certain cases some of the men who have come back have been reinstated at the old salary which they received when they enlisted. That does not seem to be fair. Their brother clerks, who have stayed at home-I am not, of course, casting the least reflection on them,-have had their increases in the usual course. I think that is a point which the Government should take up, and, if I am right in my statement of fact, the wrong should be corrected.
I should also, before sitting down, like to say one other word in support of what the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cock-shutt) said about the salaries generally of civil servants, and particularly of those in the post office, including the mail carriers. I understand the Government is considering that point, and I hope they will deal liberally with these men. There can be no doubt, with the tremendous increase in living expenses, when we are told officially that a dollar is not worth much more than fifty cents, that these men are having a
hard time. Their case is made harder by the contrast to the man who is receiving a wage, and whose wage has largely increased. I know many institutions-some of them I have to do with myself, have since the war, allowed a special war bonus, a high cost of living bonus. And while the Government, I understand, last year, did vote a special bonus of $100, that does not strike me as being sufficient to meet the needs of the men. I have had men come into my office, who were married, with large families, and lay down their family budget, and it is quite plain on the face of it, and with the knowledge I have of living expenses, that they could not get along on the salaries they receive.

With reference to section 9, concerning use of influence in getting appointments, I desire to ask the Acting Minister of Finance if there is any truth in the statement current around the city that the Auditor-General used undue influence upon the Government to have his son appointed Solicitor to the Commission, and then went personally and appeared before the Civil Service Commission, and as was stated, practically bulldozed the commission into appointing his son? The understanding is that the Government appointed him by Order in Council in the hope that the Civil Service Commission would not confirm the appointment. But the Civil Service Commission, having heard that the Government had anticipated such action, took what I take to be the proper course and refused to act in the premises until the Government would refuse to make the appointment. I ask the question, and if the minister has not the" information now, I would ask him to let me have it at a later stage.

I am not in a position to answer the question just put by the hon. gentleman. But I do not think * the Government has anything whatever to do with the matter. At any rate, I shall answer the question later.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

speechtext: Bill No. 60, to incorporate Montreal, Joliette and Transcontinental Junction Railway Company.-Mr. Denis.
Bill No. 61, respecting the Toronto, Hamilton and Buffalo Railway Company.-Mr. Stewart.

House in Committee on Bill No. 67, respecting the International Bridge and Terminal Company-Mr. Manion-Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On the preamble:
I do not see the promoter of this Bill. It would seem that very wide powers are being conferred on this company. Where is the line to be built?
Who are the incorporators?	'
I would request that these Rills be distributed so that members can follow what is going on in the committee.
The Bill has been distributed.
If the chairman of the Railway Committee can give us an explanation of this Bill, I shall be satisfied with any reasonable explanation.

This Bill, which was up before the Railway Committee, contained some contentious clauses. The railway company owning also the International Pulp 'Company at the International falls at Fort Frances', Ontario, have a railway bridge between the Canadian and American sides. This railway connects up their mills on the Canadian side. The railway crossee the bridge which the company own. This railway company and the pulp company desire to extend the railway line to a sawmill about four or five miles up or down the river-il do not know which, to provide cheap fuel for the pulp mill. They found that, under the Railway Act, they did not have the right to extend their line six miles on either side of their main line as provided in the Act. They had a charter of a bridge company which gave them a perfect right to build a railway track on the 'bridge and approaches, and they thought that, under that, they could come under the Railway Act and extend their branch lines six miles or so away from the main line on the bridge. The Board of Railway Commissioners decided that they did not possess, that power because they were not a railway with a main line. There was also, a dispute between the town of Fort Frances and this company. It appears that some 
time ago they had some' trouble, and the town compelled them to build a revetment wall along the waterfront, and they wished to run this line of railway over that waterfront. (Some clauses contained in the Bill give them the right to. run over this embankment virtually without asking the permission of the municipality, and shutting' the municipality from the wlaterfront. The municipality was represented before the Railway Board. The question was brought up there and amendments were agreed to which, I understand, were incorporated in the Bill by the clerk of the Railway Committee, and the Bill was then satisfactory to' everybody in the committee, all interests being satisfied. Mr. Alexander Smith appeared for the town.

Preamble agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

Bill No. 75, respecting the Protective Association of Canada.-Mr. Demers.
Bill No. 73, foir the relief of Frederick Ernest Zang.-<M!r. Redman.
Bill No. 74, for the relief of Thomas Bailey Wainwright.-Mr. Fripp.
The House resumed -in Committee on Bill No. 53, respecting the Civil Service of Canada-Mr. A. K. Maclean-Mir. Boivin in the Chair.

This is an innovation from the way in which appointments to the 'Civil Service have been made in previous years. That is, instead of the members undertaking the responsibility and a certain amount of worry in connection with patronage in the filling of positions, that work is now assigned to the Civil Service Commission. If that commission will give the necessary attention to this very responsible work, a considerable advance will have been made. If, however, that commission, after it undertakes the work, becomes indifferent and allows a good deal of this work to drift into the hands of the deputy ministers in the various departments, or perhaps leaves a considerable quantity of this work for the secretary to do, I question whether it will be as satisfactory as we would like to see it.
If the work drifts into the hands of the deputy ministers and the secretary, and if the commission does not give it the necessary attention, an inner circle or ring will be formed that will cause a great deal of dissatisfaction. I think, however, this is

a move in the right direction, and we should give the Bill a fair trial. If we find it is not working to the satisfaction of the members generally, some change may he made at a later date. As to beneficient action in regard to those who have voluntarily enlisted and gone overseas and those who have been drafted, I wish to compare the treatment accorded by the city of Toronto to its employees with that accorded by the Government to its employees.
I do not think the Government has treated its employees as generously	as	the city	cf	Toronto has.
At the outbreak of the war the city of Toronto continued to pay those of its employees who enlisted their full civil salaries, even in one case to the amount of $9,000 a year. These men drew their military pay as well, and some of them held pretty good positions in the army. During the second year of the war the city continued to pay them their full civil salary less the amount of their military pay, but reduced the amount of $9,000 which it was paying in one particular case, because they felt justified in making the reduction. The city of Toronto also insured for $1,000 all men enlisting in the city, iand has- paid out many hundreds of thousands of dollars in that way. This insurance is still kept up.
I have heard many complaints in connection with Government employees, and particularly in connection with the custom house. One young man that I know of in the Customs Department enlisted voluntarily and was granted both his civil and military pay, in accordance with the usual understanding that he would proceed overseas in a reasonable time. He was prepared to go overseas and so informed the department, hut after some time had elapsed and he was not sent overseas, his civil pay was cancelled and he was allowed his military pay only. The same thing occurred with six or seven others in the Customs Department. This young man to whom I have referred was made an instructor, notwithstanding his desire to go. overseas, and he still wishes to go. I got in touch with the department and suggested that he be allowed to go overseas or to revert to his civil position, but the answer was that he was to remain as instructor, and he -is still carrying out that duty, receiving only military pay. It seems to me that is hardly fair treatment from the Government. It can certainly .afford to be more generous than the city of Toronto, because of its
large revenue and its power to tax, if necessary, the lands of the whole Dominion. The city of Toronto has been very generous, and in many cases has done what really should have been done by the Government.
Many employees of the Customs Department are receiving very small pay. They have made representations to the minister oir deputy minister .at various times that they should have an .increase. I understand that many of them have not had an increase for several years. The minister may say that they were given a war bonus last year. It is true that a bonus of a hundred dollars was given, hut not to the whole stafi, for what reason I do not know. It has been represented to me that about forty members of the staff received no increase or bonus whatever, and that has created' dissatisfaction. If the Government felt they could only afford to distribute a certain amount among the employees, they should have made an equal distribution of it amongst the whole staff, instead of giving a bonus to two-thirds and nothing to the rest. I think these employees have a real grievance and I trust that in the reclassification under this Bill they will get an increase and receive the treatment they should have received long before this. The same remark applies to the post office employees, in both the inside and. the outside service, including the letter carriers. A deputation from Toronto made representations here for an increase a few weeks ago, but they received very little encouragement because the deputation was from Toronto. I understand' the Government's answer was that representations had not been made generally throughout the Dominion, but from only a few employees representing the Toronto postal employees and letter carriers. I know some of these letter carriers in Toronto who have been in the service for from twenty-five to forty years and have not received an increase for many years. Their pay, considering the high cost of living, is very small. I trust that, when this Bill is finally passed the Government will see to it that these men are treated justly, even if they are residents of Toronto. I do not think the *Government should require representations to be made generally throughout the whole Dominion. If no representations have been made by the West, it may be that conditions are better out there; perhaps they are getting better pay. I certainly think the cost of living is higher in the Bast than

in the West, and I therefore think there should be a greater increase in the East.
In the West civil servants receive an increase of fifteen per cent per annum. This is due to the fact that the cost of living is higher.

I sincerely trust that something will be done after the representations that have been made. This is a very important Bill, and inaugurates a new policy. There is to be a re-classification of the service, and a system of competitive examinations-. I think that is a step in the right direction, but it does not always follow that the person who comes out on top in the examination is best fitted for the position. I have seen in my time a young man who was extra bright and clever and who could pass the examination but who, when he was placed in a position, displayed no ability or aptitude for his work. Surely positions in any part of the country are not going to be given to people, whether they have ability or not, just because they have taken fairly high standing at an examination.
If a position should happen to be available in Ottawa, or Quebec, a young man living in Vancouver would be eligible to be examined for that position. He might be clever and pass the examination, and he might possibly be given that position. Why should you bring a man from Vancouver to fill a position in Ottawa or Quebec when you could get perhaps five hundred or a thousand people just as capable of filling that position tight in the locality? You should give consideration to the claims of those who pass the examination and who reside in the locality where the vacancy occurs. Surely amongst them you will get some who possess the ability as well as the qualifications which the passing of the examination gives them. While you insist on an examination to test the qualifications of the candidate, you should assure yourself of his ability to carry on the work successfully. It should not be left entirely to deputies or to the secretary. I am inclined to fear that a great deal of the work of selection will be assigned to subordinate officers instead of being carried on under the immediate direction of the commissioners. However, I trust I may be disappointed, and that my opinion a:s to what is likely to occur will not be verified. It may be that my judgment as to what will take place is not good. If this Bill works out in a satisfactory way we will all be perfectly satisfied and glad of the change.

Although I have read this Bill through, I am not prepared as yet to pasis on its merits or demerits. I think that probably a year's trial will disclose its weak and its strong points. There is a question that I would like to bring to the attention of the Government, and that is the position of the lower-paid public servants. I do consider, speaking more especially for the Far West, that some of our letter carriers and men in the employ of the Customs Department are quite inadequately paid. I would like to go on record as urging very strongly that they should receive a bonus or some other consideration to meet the increased cost of living. With regard to civil servants who are also soldiers, I have been very strongly opposed to those preferred soldiers. I felt that the Government had no right at any time to give a preference to any men that fought for the country, but as the Government made the contract with these men, that contract should be lived up to. If the Government's intention is to cancel all payments to those civil servants on the thirtieth of June, any men who did not fall within the operation of the Military Service Act should be allowed to break the contract on their side.
