Now, the members, to my knowledge, have always seen to it that the people they recommend for position in the Outside Service were invariably respectable people and well behaved, but what guarantee has the Government that all kinds of people will not get into the Outside Service now? There is no arrangement made that they shall be furnished with recommendations or anything of that kind. If a man seeks a position in the establishment of Sir John Eaton in Toronto what happens? The applicant has to give the names of two or three prominent citizens in the place from which he comes, and to each of these people will come a document from Eaton's saying, such a person has given your name as one who has personal knowledge of him, and accompanying it is a series of questions from the firm asking about that man, just the same as though he was recommended to .a position m the Government. That is not patronage, that is purely and simply >a guarantee that the man you recommend to Eaton's is a respectable person. You will not recommend a thief to go there. lit should be the same with the Civil Service. A man, unless he is carefully recommended, may have a record that ils not altogether too good, and the result will be 'appointments such as were made last year. Some appointments were made in certain departments of the Government without any reference to members, and to my positive knowledge-I do not want to name any party-two of the men that were appointed were' more fit for the asylum than for a job in the Civil Service, or any other service. There are all kinds of people chasing Government jobs, and the great difficulty is to select the proper party. When you do so you must shed a tear over his career, because you know he is being put in some place where he is not going to get what he deserves. There are meritorious people who do not get what they deserve, and often those who are not meritorious get a good deal more than they deserve. I think some provision should be made in the present Bill to meet the difficulties I have pointed out. The old Act that we have been working under gave the Government power by Order in Council at any time to place the outside service under the Civil Service Commission. That was all right, but no case has been made out for the great change which is

proposed' here. Whilst there has been lots of talk and questions raised about appointments, the only cases where difficulties have occurred by reason of appointments in the ridings have been where members of Parliament have deliberately placed their own friends in office. We will have the same thing here; a deputy minister will place all his relations in jobs under the Government, and the people from other parts of the country will not have anything to say about it.
What about the Auditor General?

I do not know anything about the Auditor General, who is a good old Scotchman, except that he is a very efficient officer. On several occasions in this House I have had to take his reports as proof where certain things had occurred that he would not let through. We have had him before committees on a number of occasions, and we invariably found the Auditor General was a straight and honest man. But there is a great tendency to nepotism in human nature, which extends away back to Biblical times. There is a great tendency to give jobs to your relations and I confess it is very difficult to get over at times. This tendency it will be very hard for the deputy ministers and the ministers to combat.
From my knowledge of what has taken place in this House, both when hon. gentlemen opposite were in office, and when the Conservative Party were in power, I do not think that there.were half a dozen cases brought before the House in which it could be said that wrong appointments were made through the instrumentality of the members. The member is responsible, and if he recommends an evil person to take a position everybody on the opposite side of politics in his own riding will be down on him for it. The result will be that he will have to have that appointment cancelled, or insist that whoever gets it shall walk in the straight and narrow path.
There is another thing to be considered. We are now having to deal with returned . soldiers. The Government passed an Order in. Council that no one should have a position who was of military age except a returned soldier. That was very much appreciated toy the men who are fighting the battles- of this country, whether they have returned from the front or not. Many men will return with empty sleeves and wooden legs. So far this Government has provided positions for those men, and I feel satisfied that after the clamour and excite-

*rnent of war have passed these men, without exception, will do their duty, because they have learnt the idea of discipline, which ninety per cent of 'Canadians who have not gone to the war know nothing about. Furthermore, the returned soldiers will know what efficiency is. We find that this Bill makes no provision for placing representatives of the men who are at the front on the Civil Service Commission.
I have nothing to say against the present members of the commission, but I think that provision should be made for enlarging its membership whereby at least two, if not three, members should be men who have served at the front, men who have received wounds and served their country with honour and distinction. If we do not do that what is going to happen? There are going to be examinations and we hear it said that the soldiers are going to be put at the tap of the lists, and all that sort of thing. Well, we have absolute confidence in the present members of the Civil Service Commission, but none of those gentlemen have a permanent lease of life. I would not like to is-e-e them disappear, but - they are not going to live forever, and their places will be taken by others who may have no sympathy with the war or with the soldiers. The result will 'be that the soldier will 'be constantly cheated out of office by trick examinations. For that reason I would ask the minister to put representatives of the returned soldiers on the commission to see that there is no such thing as trick examinations imposed on the returned soldiers.
There are other departments! of the Government in the Inside Service where examinations have to be passed. I do not wish to mention any names, but unless a man. belongs to. a union he gets a trick examination and has no chance to get an appointment. If he belongs to a certain union, he has every chance, and if he does not belong to that order he is out in the cold. So, in this case, if you are going to give a preference to a returned soldier, and you are honest about it, and the House is honest about it, then make provision that there shall be people on this commission who will fight for the returned soldier and see that he gets his proper due. I think these are sentiments which should touch the heart of gentlemen who are sitting within the sound olf my voice, and I am not asking too much when I ask that this board be enlarged. I have no right to iask for the expenditure of a larger amount of money than the Government is providing for this measure; I would be called to ord>er by the chairman if I did. But perhaps we could have some soldiers put on. that commission who would serve for nothing and not ask fohsalaries.
I. want to refer to another point in connection with the returned soldier. The matter has been referred to by the hon. member for 'London (Mr. Cronyn), who has placed his case very clearly before the House. I have spoken already this session on this matter, and perhaps it would not be right for me to say another word. I only desire to answer the suggestions that have been made that the men who went to the front in 1914 should he asked to return and revert to the Civil Service, give up all they fought for in France, or else give up their salaries. That would affect four generals .at the front, who went over there as juniors and have received their crossed swords on the battlefield. They were men of the permanent corps holding 'Civil Service appointments. You ask these men, who are highly- -qualified officers, many of them the best officers we have, to return under this regulation, men who have been engineers in the service, qualified as artillerymen and observers. You say to them: We don't want you to serve your country any longer, you must give up what you have there and come back.
What would they get when they came back? I know one officer who went over as a permanent non.-com. in the service, a corporal of the permanent corps when he left. He went to Europe, distinguished himself, and rose to the rank of major. Through illness he w.as invalided to Canada. Whilst he was recovering an order went forth that no officers who were invalided to Canada were to be allowed to go to the front from here, and he had to remain at .home. He was not willing to do so. But what were the conditions under which be returned to duty? Although he had won his commission and crowns on the other side, he had to go back in the permanent corps as a corporal. There is no guarantee, and there has been no guarantee, provided by this Government for any man who has left for the front from the permanent corps or militia and who obtains a promotion abroad. When he comes back he reverts exactly to the rank in the army or the militia he had before the war. This Parliament might very well -have given consideration to amendments to the Militia Act in justice to officers who have gone overseas and won their promotion. But we are in a hurry to get away from here and important matters have been forgotten. If hon. gentlemen waver in the



right, .and will not live up to its .obligations, as a man. who represents the soldiers in this House I insist on justice and that the contracts are carried out. Sir John Eaton is not asking, nor is any other of the great business houses of the country, to get out of the voluntary contracts they have made with the men who left their employ for the front, and they are paying the wives what was promised when the men left. Surely this (House of Commons has not degenerated so much since the war began that it wants *to do what is a rank injustice and a breach of contract so far as the men at the front are concerned.
There are one or two other matters in connection with this Bill which I think it would be well to consider seriously before proceeding to give it its final touches, and I hope the minister will take them home to-night, and bring in a few amendments', especially that there shall be representatives of the returned soldiers appointed on the commission. We all express so much sympathy for the returned soldiers here, but he gets so little of it when it comes to practice. It is time we did something more than talk about it. There is another clause in the Bill which deals with technical men. Technical men are the young fellows who come from the universities as draughtsmen, surveyors and designers, and enter the departments, nearly all of them with the Bachelor of Science degree. They are put in Class 2 according to this Bill. Why should the best brains which enter the service-chemists, draughtsmen and men of ability-be put into the Second Division? The Bill provides that architects and draughtsmen shall be put in that division, and the hardship of it is that these men, according to the Bill, can never be put into the First Division, can never become heads of departments. I hope the minister will reconsider that. I want to assure him right now, from my experience all over the country, and from my experience as to what the soldiers are saying, the men I suppose chiefly interested in the Bill, they do not think there is any great necessity for .all this row about putting the Outside Civil Service under a commission. That is going to be a tremendous work. It should be undertaken after the war is over, when we would have plenty of time to pass a carefully
9 p.m. considered Bill. It has not been proven that there is any merit whatever in what is known as Civil Service reform, because in England and in the United States they have had to put the best men in the country at the head of their

departments. Charles M. Schwab was put the other day at the head of the ship construction.
Mr. Schwab has not entered the Civil Service. He has entered the public service, just as Sir Auckland Geddes did in England.
He is the head of a department.
And so is Geddes. Mr. Sehwa,b has not become a member of the Civil Service.

Of course, these men would not ithipik of becoming members of the [DOT]Civil Service. Why should men like that want to enter the Civil Service? My observation is when it comes down to the point where we need real men we cannot get them from, the 'Civil Service. Therefore, as f.ax as this Bill is concerned, I d'o not think it has justified so xmuch stupid talk about it. I heard the speech of the hon. member for P.arkdiale (Mr. Mowat) this afternoon. And I thought if that was all that could be said on behalf of the Bill there was not very much to be said. If you pass this Bill you will get whole groups of men in office, and you make no provision to get rid of them if they aie of no use. Neither the deputy head nor iany other sub-head has any authority to dismiss a man or to establish discipline in the service, not even the minister. That is dealt with by the Govern-nor General in Council. Suppose a man away out in the country will not do what he has been ordered to do: the superior refers the matter .to the officer next higher np; that officer passes it on to the deputy minister, and the deputy to the minister; the minister puts it before the Cabinet and the Cabinet has to. decide whether a postmaster drawing $25 a year shall he dismissed. The whole thing, to my mind, is absurd. The Bill should be better framed than it is. I do not think any..argument has been advanced by either the minister or anybody in this House which has satisfied me that there is any crying desire for Civil Service reform of this kind. The ery for reform comes altogether from those people who have failed to get appointments.

I was quite surprised to hear the member for Parkdale (Mt. Mowat) say -this afternoon that this Bill would be unpopular. As far as my observations go it is popular with pretty nearly every class in the community. I do not know any class of people with whom it should be so popular as the members of this House. I

congratulate the minister upo-n the Bill which he has brought down. It is not perfect, but I do not think we should look for perfection in legislation enacted1 by human beings. However, I wish to bring to the attention of the minister a few of the imperfections by which I have been impressed.
I heartily approve of the principle laid down in the Bill that the returned soldier should be taken care of. In many parts of the country institutions are training returned soldiers who intend to take up' different occupations from those in which they were engaged before they went to the war. Many men who were not in the Civil Service before they went to the front may on their return prepare for .and perform efficiently the duties of civil servants, and in this respect there is work for the Department of Soldiers' Re-Establishment. These men have risked their lives, endured all kinds of hardship and, in some cases, of misery, in order to protect our homes, and if there is any classs of people to whom we isihould give special consideration it is the men who return from the war. This Bill provides that even if such men are not as well qualified on the competitive examination as some others may be, they are eligible for appointment. That is only fair, and I believe that such men will be most. efficient. I hope that the Civil Service Commission will make that a particular feature of their work and that they will give the closest attention to it.
I was much impressed by the remarks made by the member for Brantford (Mr. Coekshutt). It will not be satisfactory to send from Ottawa, Toronto, Hamilton or other eastern centres, men to take up Government positions, say, in Calgary or Edmonton. Those in the locality concerned who are qualified should receive special consideration. I do not say this because I want to have anything to do with appointments in Toronto; I am delighted to be relieved of that responsibility. But the local feeling with regard to appointments of this kind should	receive
the consideration of the Government. The. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) emphasized the wide power that is conferred upon deputy ministers. I want to get away from patronage; I believe that that is the sentiment of the people. But if the people are forced to choose between the patronage system and a family-compact system, they will prefer the former. Nothing is more repugnant to public sentiment than the filling-of public offices with men connected by blood relationship, or by marriage

with some particular group of officials. This Bill puts it in the power of deputy ministers practically to take care of every relative they have, and every relative their wives have, and1 every person he is connected with in any way.

How?
Mr. HOC'KEN: These appointments are made on the recommendation of the deputy minister. The man getting the highest marks in the competitive examination is appointed on probation, and if at the end of six months or a year the deputy minister wants to give the appointment to the second man on the list, who happens to be a friend of his, the probationary period may be ended with the dismissal of the man who was highest in the examination.
The. selection is made by the Civil Service Commission. The deputy minister may dismiss, but there is an appeal to the Civil Service Commission. The probation is for a period of six months or a year.

That is as I understand it. Let us suppose the second man on the list is the man the deputy minister wants.
I do not charge deputy ministers with being concerned in any corrupt act, but they are just as human as we are, and if the man who comes second is a relative or friend of the deputy minister the probationary period of the highest man may end in a report by the deputy minister to the Civil Service Commission that his services are unsatisfactory; and the commission sends along the next man. The best man to determine the qualification or fitness of an employee is the deputy minister; I do not see how we can get away from that. But I should like to see in this Bill a provision that the annual report of the Civil Service Commission shall state not only the "name -. of the appointee, his salary, and so on, but also how many relatives he had by blood or by marriage in the service. In that way a check would be put on those who are disposed for one reason dr andther to create a family compact.

If the deputy has the appointment, does that not mean that the minister will have something to say about it? because the minister has power to retire his deputy if the latter does not play the game. Moreover, is it not simply a left-handed way of letting the ministers have the patronage, instead of the members of Parliament?

The appointment is made by the Civil Service Commission, but power

is vested in the deputy minister to eliminate one man after another who may be so appointed by the commission. The suggestion which I have made would put a check on the deputy minister in the matter of his appointing half a dozen men of one family to positions in the service. If an investigation were made -of the service here in Ottawa, it would he found that in some cases half a dozen different members of the same family are in the service, sometimes in the same department. They may be qualified, but the principle is repugnant to the feelings of the people. It is the last thing we should encourage, or even permit, and if it cannot be absolutely prevented, it should at least be discouraged by such a plan as I have suggested. Then, take the appointments for which no examination is possible. I assume tlqat professional and technical men would include carpenters, plumbers, printers and men of that kind. The appointment of such men rests with the deputy minister, who makes recommendation to the commission. The Deputy Minister of Public Works, for instance, would have the appointment of I do not know how many carpenters and plumbers all over the Dominion;	.
Technical men are men of special or scientific knowledge- of mining, fisheries, and things of that kind. The expression "technical officers" would not include tradesmen.

What examination can the Civil Service Commission set for carpenters? One carpenter is equal to another. How are you going to determine superiority of qualifications amongst men of that class? The same applies to printers and plumbers, large numbers of whom are employed. That responsibility all rests upon the deputy ministers, and that is altogether too much power to put into their hands, unless there is some additional check than that which is provided in the Bill as it stands at present.
The Commission will find a method of appointing men of that class. The deputy minister has nothing to do with it.
I do not understand that from the Bill.

I could not help feeling, while the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Ho-cken) was speaking about the influence that might be exercised by a deputy minister, that, as a rule, deputy

ministers are not so unkind to their relatives as to wish to have them placed in the Civil Service. I have had some knowledge of the Civil Service for a few years, and, from my experience, my advice to my friends and acquaintances has been to keep clear of the Civil Service above anything else. If you have any ambition; if you ever expect to make any headway in the world; if you place- any value on your initiative, your freedom, then, for Heaven's sake, steer clear of the Civil Service. If you want to become part of a machine by which you move along without exercising your initiative, then the Civil Service is the proper place for you. My sympathies have always been with those employed in the Civil Service. I want it distinctly understood that, if to-night I -say -anything that may, in some measure, reflect upon civil servants, I -have no intention of casting any reflection on any one who is at present or who may in the future'be in the Service. When the minister was pointing out the difference between the position occupied by Mr. Schwab and Mr. Geddes and the position, of those -in the Civil Service, it struck me that the difference was possibly an imaginary one. The minister told us that the former were in the public service, whereas the latter were in the Civil Service.

What I meant was that Mr. Schwab was appointed head of the Shipbuilding Commission because he had some knowledge of that particular business. The civil servants of the United States Government have no opportunity of gaining a knowledge of building ships. That is not their business. It is, therefore, only natural that -somebody should he taken from the outside. There is -quite a distinction.

I quite understand what >the minister had in -mind. In the positions in which Mr. Schw-aJb . and Mr. Geddes were placed, they were able to exercise their initiative, to -do things and to control those placed under them. Some hon-. members who- spoke dealt with civil servants who enlisted voluntarily and went overseas with the first and second contingents, and with whom the Government entered into a contract to pay them their Civil -Service salaries in addition to their military pay. I think that almost without exception those who spoke in reference to that matter said that it would be a -bre-ach of contract on the part of the Government with those men -if that contract was not carried out to the very letter. I hardly

look at the matter in that light. We are, at the present time, passing through a condition of change. The 'war has revolutionized everything in the world. Conditions today are not what they were six months ago or a year .ago. Changes are rapidly taking place. When these men entered the military service, we had the volunteer system. Today we have compulsory military service in this country. While it would he advisable and obligating to carry out that contract with men not eligible under the Military Service Act, as regards any man who is today eligible for service under the Military Service Act, I do not consider that this Government or any other is justified in giving him preference over any one else. The same argument applies to the clamour that is .being raised to-day throughout the country with regard to the cancellation of exemption of farmers. Some safeguards might be provided whereby, in certain instances, where a great hardship is going to ensue, exemptions might be made; but in so far as keeping faith with those men is concerned, changed war conditions have relieved the Government of any such responsibility. The -very fact that we have to-day in Canada . compulsory military service does not justify the Government in singling out civil servants and paying them salaries, in addition to their military pay. Every one in this country ought to be on an equal footing with regard to this war. We ought to. have, in so far as is possible, an equality of service and of sacrifice on the part of every one.
In my opinion, this is a most inopportune time for the introduction of a Bill respecting the Civil Service of Canada. There is no justification for taking any^ class of the people in this country or in any other country and cuddling them along and placing safeguards around them so that they are safeguarded from competition with other people. You give them privileges that other people do not enjoy, and you do a great deal of harm in that respect. It is true you kill, you strangle initiative in them, and in that way you do a grgat deal of injury to them. I should' like to see, if it were only possible, some way of providing for promotion for merit in the Civil Service. I do not believe that has always been the custom, and I do. not think it will be possible under this Bill.
By placing the Outside Service in the hands of the Civil Service Commission, we are departing from an established rule that has. been in existence in the British Empire for many years; that is, responsible and representative government. I believe a
government ought to he responsible to the people for the administration of the [DOT]affairs of the country. I do not believe you can delegate those responsibilities to any commission and say: The commission have done so and so; the Government cannot interfere in the matter, and we are not responsible for the action of the commission. We have not had a great deal of experience in Canada with regard to commissions; but there is at the present time a feeling so intense burning in the veins of our people with regard to one commission that h is been appointed in Canada, that it should cause us to hesitate, to reflect as to what the consequence may be of placing another commission in a position in which they will be able to exercise as much authority as that one is empowered to exercise, and I see that the powers are almost identical. You may rest assured that until some very serious misdemeanour is committed the Government will not call for the resignation of a member of any commission. As long as we have responsible and representative government in this country, responsibility rests upon the members who are elected to represent the people in Parliament, and a commission should not be beyond the reach of those so elected. I do not think it is right or fair that such power should he placed outside the control of the representatives of the people. A great deal has been said about the abuses that have crept in in connection with the distribution of patronage. While it may be true of certain constituencies where there is a great deal of patronage, in the inland counties, one of which I represent, there is little or no patronage,' and I do not, as a result, hold the same views on this matter that some others do. I know that if the Civil Service Commission have the right to select some one to occupy a position in the county where I live, and some one was brought in from some outside place to fill a vacancy, the people of my constituency would be very indignant indeed, and justly so, and that is the very thing likely to occur under this Act. I received in my mail only the other morning a notice from the Civil Service Commission that applications would be received for the position of postmaster at Lethbridge, and I can imagine what the consequences would be if some one from Oxford was selected to fill that position. But this is likely to happen under present conditions. My hon. fxiend from West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) has spoken of the influence that may he exerted on behalf of friends, and it may be that some would like to see a friend who was

not competent to fill any other place secure a position where he could be taken care of. I think there is greater danger of abuses under this Bill than under the old system. So far as the constituency I represent is concerned, I do not think I have secured the appointment of more than two from that constituency during the seven years I have been its representative, so I have no need to feel anxious about the number of appointments that would come to that constituency. In one case I recommended a very able and competent young man who had the qualifications for almost any position. He was taken on, and was later put on the permanent staff, and if ever a man was crucified that man was, and he will regret to his dying day that he ever entered the service, and I also regret ever recommending him-for that position. Outside of the two I have mentioned, two others were appointed in the railway mail service, and that is the amount of the patronage that has come to the constituency of -South Oxford during the last seven years, and I do not anticipate there would be much more come to it in the next six or seven years -if conditions remained as they were under the old Act. So I do not speak of this measure with the feeling that it will affect me in any way if I should continue ito represent that constituency.
I am -speaking in this way because I feel this is an inopportune time to introduce a measure of this kind when we have coming back from overseas every day men who are maimed for life, and who will find it difficult to follow their old vocation. These men should surely be given the preference, but I cannot see within the four corners of the Bill anything to safeguard their rights in any degree. It is true that an Order in Council has been passed, but so far as the Bill itself is concerned-I have looked it over very carefully-no safeguards have been provided. On the contrary, the examinations that may be prescribed by the Civil Service Commission will probably debar a great many of these men from entering the Civil Service, who under -present conditions might be appointed. Why is- it that to-day practically the only positions you can get for a returned isoldier are caretakers of public buildings or some other menial employment of that kind? It may be that in other parts of the country returned soldiers are being given positions, but I am speaking of what is taking place In the rural districts and smaller towns and cities.

Reference has been made to the appointment of registrars in connection with the registration of man-power. I wish to say that if the appointments made are as satisfactory as in the city which I represent, namely, the City of .Saskatoon- although I had nothing to do with it-every person will be perfectly happy. I notice from a newspaper received to-day that a returned soldier was appointed in the city of Saskatoon. In my opinion that appointment is a very worthy one and will undoubtedly prove satisfactory.
There seems to be a great deal of fear as to the appointments to be made by the Civil Service Commission. My experience as a member only dates from the 17th of December last, and if other horn, gentlemen have had the same experience as myself-even although I have not had numerous applicants for positions-they will feel very pleased to foe rid of the responsibility of having to recommend men for positions in the service. Viewed from any angle, the change which is proposed ought to afford members great relief. Judging from the experience of the past, for every friend a member makes when he recommends an .appointment, there will be forty or fifty disgrunitled1 constituents. Therefore, I do not think any member should feel that he is being deprived of a privilege but rather of a burden to be relieved of patronage. We want to see the public service run on business principles, and in that way obtain the best results. In my opinion the method proposed by the Bill tends to bring that about, and we may therefore look for a great improvement in the public service.

I was reminded of my own position by the observations of the hon. member for East York (Mr. Foster) that he was consulted about a certain appointment, and after he had given his views they were not followed. I was not looking for or expecting any patronage; but the returning officer appointed in my county last year, appointed., of course, without consulting me, was a very good respectable Tory. They appointed sixty enumerators also, every one of them Tories of the highest orthodoxy. We were told that everything was to be "fifty-fifty," but that is the kind of " fifty-fifty " we got. I

did not complain; I was not disappointed; I was looking for that kind of thing. After appointing this returning officer-and I hold the acting minister (Mr. A. K. Maclean) responsible for it, he is the only minister we have in the province except the Prime Minister, who has other things to look after; patronage of this kind, I believe, is handled by the Acting Minister of Finance.
What kind of patronage?

Later I was asked to say if the man appointed returning officer would be satisfactory to me. I wrote back: Certainly. When L was going to get Tory anyhow, I preferred a decent Tory; so I said, yes, the old man was good enough for me. But was he appointed? No, he was too good, too decent. They went to the poorest kind of a Tory they could get and appointed him over the head of the other man. So* I sympathize with my good friend who is disappointed, for I am in exactly the same position.
Not exactly. In my case tlhe man is a returned soldier who should have been appointed.

There has been a lot of talk about patronage to-night directed at this Bill, but it has not hit at the mairk at all. The patronage which is objected to is not the few appointments made by the member. I have been in control of the patronage in my constituency for four or five years, and I don't think I secured appointments for more than one person each year to post offices and so on, and there never has been a complaint against one of them, although I turned down dozens and dozens of men. That is not what the people are kicking so much about to-day, but rather at the matter of letting contracts to friends at exorbitant prices with the object of having some of the money turned back to the party funds. I do not see anything in this Bill to remedy that state of affairs. That is the big thing the people mean by " patronage," and not the few appointments made here and theie by members. When there is an appointment to be made of a postmaster in some rural constituency, who knows better than the member where that post office should he situated if a new post office is to bb opened up? I think that members*, with the majority they have behind them this year, and the independence which characterizes members in this House, would feel that they could defy their constituency, or 
one or two people here and there, and be big enough to locate the offices where they would best serve the community. There is an injustice done here, and under this so-called reform havoc will be wrought in the Civil Service and a great deal of displeasure and more harm caused. I think that, where there is more than one application for a postmaster, at least the opinion of the member should be taken. It is not only a matter of shifting a man into this department or into that. The Bill as constituted is an excellent thing. But where there are more than two applications for a post office, or where there is a vacancy for a postmaster caused by the opening of a new office or by death, I think the member could be consulted first and no harm result. If this Bill is to fulfil the promises* of the Government, something should be put in it to provide that every tender for dredging or any other work or for any supplies should be sealed and left in a designated place until the time comes to open it, and it should be opened in public. In that way we will get away from patronage in the big sense of the word.
That is provided for in other legislation, by Order in Council. It has nothing to do with the Civil Service Commission.

That is a form of patronage that may well be embodied in this Bill instead of in an Order in Council. I am not taking up the cudgels about Orders in Council; I have endorsed some of them. But this is going out as a Civil Service Bill, and is not a complete reform of patronage.
I have no* doubt that the intention of the Government, as enacted by Order in Council, will be followed out faithfully and to the letter, and that the lowest tenderer will receive the contract in each case. That would, accomplish the strict abolition, of patronage.

As* many members began work in committees at ten o'clock this morning, and it is now midnight, and I assume we will be adjourning before long,
I do not wish to take up very much time. With the general .principle of the Bill I am in hearty agreement, as I said when, it was (first introduced. Anybody who was born in Ottawa and has lived here all his life, and who has had anything to
12	m, do with politics must assuredly welcome any measure to put an end to patronage. The very fact that a man has been born in Ottawa and lived here all

his life and has had something to do with politics makes him look at a measure of this kind even with a more pritical eye than that -of my hon. friend from Winnipeg (Mr. Blake), who has just spoken. I agree with him that what the public understand in the talk' about patronage is the wider meaning covering every kind of distribution of party or Government favours such as my hon. friend indicated.
The prevention of graft.

The hon. minister who
is in charge of this Bill read to the committee a statement from the Civil Service Commission purporting to detail what they have done since February 13 last, when the management of the Civil Service was practically turned over to them-and as my hon. friend said just now this Bill proposes to give statutory authority for the power that was then vested in the Civil Service Commission. I presume that, owing to a rush of work, the Civil Service Commission overlooked an important part of their work with which I think I should acquaint the committee, because I think it has an important bearing on the Bill. It has this bearing on the Bill, that unless something is done to give the House and the public some assurance that different methods will prevail, the^ Civil Service Commission is not likely to meet the views and the wishes of the people who desire that patronage should be abolished. The Order in Council transferring the management of Civil Service affairs to the commission was passed on February 13 last, I understood my hon.' friend to say. On February 18, five days after the commission was put in sole charge, they issued a circular and blank form, which I hold in my hand, and on which applicants for positions were expected to give their name, address, age, position desired, experience, and itwo classes of references, one as to ability and one as to character and habits. In the city of Ottawa, I am informed, hundreds of these forms were sent out, and each person who received one received at the same time a circular from the Civil Service Commission in these terms:
The enclosed form of application for temporary employment is sent you at the instance of Mr. A. E. Fripp, M.P.
No!

Yes.
It should be filled in and returned to the Office of the Civil Service Commission.
Patronage was supposed to have been abolished by this Order in Council on February 13 last.
Who issued that letter?
The Civil Service Commission.

It is an application form? Mr. MURPHY:	Yes, and a covering
letter is sent with it.

It does not sound like anything that would come from the Civil Service Commission. I do not doubt that the letter is authentic, but I hardly imagine that it was issued by the Civil Service Commission.

Unhappily these things
are judged not by sounds but by words. '

I am assured that that
is where it came from and that the forms, as this circular states, were to be filled in and sent to the commission.
Is that the original document?

Yes; I will send it to my hon. friend. Even assuming that this circular was not sent out by the Civil Service Commission, it requests that the forms shall he filled in and sent to that body. The Civil Service Commission, therefore, cannot be absolved of all connection with the transaction.

It may not have been very objectionable, anyway. Perhaps the Civil Service Commission desired to establish a list of those who would he available for temporary employment in Ottawa. Quite likely they have lists in some of the departments, hut the commission may have required further information. I will make inquiries and say something a-bout the matter to-morrow.

The reason suggested
by my hon. friend is a most extraordinary one. What necessity was there for the Civil Service Commission sending out a circular saying " the enclosed form of application for temporary employment is sent to you at the instance of Mr. A. E. Fripp, M.P.." If this was done because of the reason suggested by my hon. friend, that the commission desired to establish a list of those desiring temporary employment-
I did not say the Civil Service Commission sent it out.

Why the mention in this circular that it was sent out at the instance

of Mr. Fripp? These forms, when signed, were returned to the Civil Service Commission, which, on the date on which this letter was issued, February 18, were in complete control of the situation. The Civil Service Commission will be no more in control of the situation after the passing of this Act, than they were on the date mentioned. What guarantee have we in the Act that practices such as this will not be continued after the Act shall have been put in force? I do not cite this occurrence for the purpose of objecting to the Act or of putting any obstacle in the way of bringing about the reform that we all desire. 1 am simply pointing out that even after this reform was supposed to have been instituted, we had an occurrence such as the one that I have acquainted the committee with. I am told that these forms were sent to hundreds of people in Ottawa. I draw this to my hon. friend's attention so that the matter may be considered during the discussion of the Bill and so that some provision or provisions may be inserted in the Bill whereby the public wall have a guarantee that neither the Civil Service Commission, nor a member of Parliament, nor any individual can do anything, of this kind in the future. The acting minister will agree with that most heartily, because I am sure that he is seriously desirous of effecting the reforms which this Bill aims at. Like some other hon. gentlemen, I have been disappointed that those on the other side who have criticised the Bill- because the discussion has been carried on chiefly by supporters of the Government- did not offer some suggestions to take the place of the sections to which they have objected. Possibly that may be done in future; in any event I hope it will.
